transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, honestly, doctor, I... I just don't know how much longer I can keep pushing through my days like this. I came in because I am just tired all the time. And I mean all the time. It’s not just the normal kind of tired you get after a long week, you know? I’ve been a claims adjuster for a long time, and I know the job can be demanding with all the paperwork and the back-and-forth, but lately... well, it’s just overwhelming. 

I get to the office, sit down at my desk, and by midmorning—literally just a couple of hours into the shift—after just reviewing a few standard files or maybe walking a junior adjuster through a claim, I am completely done. It feels like my body and my brain are already just running on empty. And it’s so frustrating because it's only 10:30 in the morning and I still have a whole day ahead of me, dozens of appraisals to look at, people asking me questions, and I just have absolutely nothing left in the tank. I just sit there staring at the screen, and it takes everything in me just to keep my eyes focused and pretend I'm functioning. I thought maybe I just needed a weekend to catch up, but this exhaustion just clings to me every single day, and I just can't seem to shake it no matter what I do.
Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy?

Well, that's... that's the thing, isn't it? I mean, I try. I really do. My husband, bless him, he tries so hard to cheer me up. He'll suggest we cook dinner together, maybe have the kids over, make a whole family evening out of it. And we used to do that all the time. I used to love it. The kitchen would be chaotic, everyone talking over each other, the smell of garlic and onions cooking... it was wonderful. 

But now? Most days, it just feels like there’s this... this heavy, gray film over everything. Even when he's being so sweet and kind, or when everyone is laughing in the kitchen, I'm just standing there, chopping vegetables or stirring a pot, completely going through the motions. I can smile when I'm supposed to, and I can say the right things, but I don't actually feel it anymore. The enjoyment, the warmth... it just doesn't reach me. It's like I'm watching my own life happen from behind a dirty window. I know I should be happy in those moments, I know I used to be, but I just feel so flat and disconnected from it all. And it's not just cooking, it's... well, it's pretty much everything. It’s just this constant, dull feeling that never really lifts, no matter what we’re doing.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Actually, no, which is... well, it's almost confusing to me. You would think, with how absolutely drained I feel every single minute of the day, that my sleep would be all over the place. But my sleep is actually fine. I don't have any trouble falling asleep at all. Usually, by the time 10:00 rolls around, I am just so desperate to get into bed and just turn off for a while. 

My husband, he’s the one who tosses and turns—he has to have the ceiling fan on a certain speed, and he’s always adjusting the blankets, getting up to check his phone—but me? Once my head hits that pillow, I am out. I sleep like a rock. I don't even wake up in the middle of the night to use the restroom or get a drink of water or anything like that, which I know a lot of women my age complain about. I sleep a solid eight, sometimes even nine hours if it's the weekend and I don't have to log in for work. 

But... and this is the most frustrating part of it all... even after sleeping that deeply for that long, when my alarm goes off at 6:00 AM, I feel like I haven't slept a wink. I just lie there looking at the ceiling, feeling like my limbs weigh a hundred pounds. So, no, the actual act of sleeping isn't the problem at all, I can fall asleep and stay asleep just fine. It just doesn't seem to do me any good whatsoever.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite lately?

You know, I was just thinking about that... well, actually, my husband brought it up the other day because he was worried I might not be eating enough, but... no, I wouldn't say my appetite has changed at all. It's funny because you'd think, with how absolutely drained I am all the time, that I'd either be eating everything in sight trying to find some quick energy, or just skipping meals entirely because it's too much effort to even chew. 

But I still eat my normal meals. Like, every single morning, I have my oatmeal. I've been eating the same maple and brown sugar oatmeal for, gosh, probably fifteen years now. I just pop it in the microwave before I log on for work, and I always finish the whole bowl. And then for lunch, I usually have a turkey sandwich or maybe some leftovers from the night before. I just eat it right there at my desk while I'm looking at the claims files. I don't really taste it much these days, to be perfectly honest with you. It’s just like I was saying earlier about cooking dinner with the family—the food is just... there. It's just fuel to get me to the next hour. 

But I do eat it. I finish my plate at dinner, too. Like, my husband made this lovely roast chicken on Sunday with those little red potatoes and the baby carrots, and I ate a completely normal portion. I didn't go back for seconds, but I didn't leave anything on my plate either. So, no, I haven't been skipping meals or eating more than usual. The actual enjoyment of the food is definitely gone, but the amount I'm putting in my mouth? No, that's stayed exactly the same as it always has been.
Do you have trouble concentrating on things like reading or work tasks?

Well, yes... yes, I do. And it's really starting to become a problem, honestly. I mean, my job—I'm a claims adjuster, right? So my whole day is looking at files, reading through reports, checking details, comparing statements to policies. It’s exactly the kind of work where you have to be sharp. You have to catch the little things. But lately... it's like my brain is just moving through molasses. 

I'll be looking at a file, one I’ve probably seen a hundred variations of over the years, and I'll realize I've read the same paragraph four times and I have no idea what it said. I’m starting to miss things, little details in the audits that I never used to miss. And it takes me so much longer to sign off on a file now. I just sit there staring at the screen, trying to force myself to focus, but my mind just kind of drifts into this gray fog. I used to be so efficient, you know? I prided myself on it. But now, I'm just constantly terrified I'm going to make a huge mistake because I just can't hold my concentration together. 

And it's not just work, either. It bleeds into everything else. I used to paint—just watercolors, nothing professional, but I loved it. And my husband and I used to go hiking on the weekends, or I'd volunteer at the local animal shelter on Saturday mornings. But I've completely pulled back from all of that. I haven't touched my brushes in months. I just... I don't have the mental energy for it. By the time the workday is over, or the weekend finally gets here, I'm just so depleted from trying to force myself to focus all week that I can't even fathom trying to concentrate on a painting or even just paying attention to where I'm walking on a trail. I'm just... I'm just trying to survive the week, you know? Just trying to get from Monday to Friday without completely falling apart, so all those extra things, the things that actually take focus and energy outside of work, they've just completely fallen by the wayside.
Have you been feeling guilty or worthless about anything lately?

Well... guilty? Worthless? No, not exactly. I mean, I don't sit around thinking I'm a terrible person or anything like that. It's not like I feel like I've committed some awful crime or that I don't deserve to be here. It's not that sharp, if that makes sense. It's more just... a dull disappointment, I guess? 

Like, I know my husband misses how we used to be. I can see it in his face when Friday night rolls around and he asks if I want to go to that little Italian place we used to love downtown, and I just tell him I'm too tired and want to stay in. He always says it's fine, that he understands, but I know it's not fine. I know I'm not the fun, energetic wife I used to be. And the kids—they're grown, of course, out on their own, but when they call on Sundays, I feel like I have nothing interesting to say to them anymore because I don't *do* anything. 

But I wouldn't call it guilt, really. Guilt feels like an active emotion, like something that would require energy. And feeling worthless... no, I know I have value. I know I'm a good mother, a good wife, I know I'm competent at my job, even if I'm struggling with it right now. It's just that I feel so incredibly flat. I don't feel guilty about being flat, I just feel... resigned to it, almost. Like this is just how it is now. So, no, I don't think I'm having those kinds of thoughts, not the way you're describing them. I just feel like a watered-down version of myself, but I don't hate myself for it. I'm just too tired for that.
Have you noticed any changes in your weight recently?

Well, no, not at all actually. Which I suppose makes perfect sense when you think about what I was just saying about my meals, right? Since I’m eating the exact same oatmeal and the exact same sandwiches day in and day out, my weight has just stayed completely static. 

I actually have this routine—I step on the scale in the master bathroom every Monday morning right before I get in the shower. It’s just a habit I started decades ago, back when I was trying to lose the baby weight after my youngest was born, and I just never stopped doing it. So every Monday, I look down, and it’s the exact same number. It’s been hovering right around that same spot for... oh, gosh, it has to be at least five or six years now. My clothes all fit exactly the same, too. The slacks I wear when I actually have to go into the office instead of working from home, they button just fine—no tighter, no looser. 

My husband actually asked me about this, too, a few weeks ago when he was getting all worried about my appetite, but I told him, you know, just look at me. I haven't shrunk, I haven't expanded. It’s just... unchanging. I suppose a lot of women my age might be thrilled to not be gaining weight, especially considering I sit at a desk all day and I've completely stopped doing any of that hiking I used to do, but I can't even muster up the energy to care about it. It’s just a number on the scale that never moves. So, no, to answer your question, no weight changes whatsoever.
Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to be alive or of harming yourself?

Oh, no. No, no, no. Never anything like that. I know people get depressed and they... they go to that dark place, but that's just not me. It's never been me. I mean, I'm Catholic, for one thing—raised Catholic, anyway, even if I haven't been to Mass since my mother passed away back in 2018. But you know, that kind of upbringing, it sticks with you. The whole idea of... well, of doing something like that, it's just completely off the table. It's not even a thought that crosses my mind. 

And like I was saying before, I don't feel worthless. I don't feel like a burden. I know my husband needs me, even if I'm not much fun right now. He's terrible with the finances, for example. If I weren't here, he'd probably forget to pay the property taxes on the house, and then where would he be? And my kids, even though they're grown and out in the world, they still call me every Sunday. My daughter just got engaged last month, actually. She's planning a spring wedding, and she's already asking me about venues and catering and all of that. I can't even imagine not being here for that. I mean, I don't have the energy to actually *help* her plan it right now, which makes me feel a little guilty, I suppose—even though I told you I didn't feel guilty, maybe I do, just a tiny bit about that. But the point is, I want to be there. I want to see her walk down the aisle. 

So, no, I don't want to die. I don't want to hurt myself. I just... I just want to feel like *me* again. I want to wake up and actually look forward to the day instead of just bracing myself for it. I want to be able to read a file at work and actually comprehend it the first time. I just want this heavy, gray blanket to lift off of me. But I'm certainly not going to do anything drastic. I'm just tired, doctor. Just so, so tired. But I'm going to keep putting one foot in front of the other, just like I do every Monday through Friday. I just wish it wasn't so hard.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Oh, gosh, let me think... it's been quite a while now. I know I said I feel like a watered-down version of myself, and honestly, it feels like I've been this way for... well, it's been about three years and three months. 

I know the exact timeline because it started right around the time things changed at work. I'm a claims adjuster, you see, and I had been doing the standard desk work for years—handling my own files, dealing with the auto claims, just keeping my head down and doing my job. But then, about three years and three months ago, they decided to completely restructure the department. They moved me into this higher-responsibility role. Suddenly, I wasn't just handling my own claims anymore; I was supposed to be mentoring the newer adjusters, answering all their questions, reviewing their files before they could authorize payouts. 

And on top of that, they rolled out this massive new workflow system. It was supposed to be more efficient, paperless, all cloud-based, but it was just a nightmare. I was put in charge of overseeing how my team adapted to it. So, instead of just doing my work, I was troubleshooting software glitches, trying to explain protocols to twenty-somethings who didn't understand the basics of liability, and dealing with management breathing down my neck about productivity metrics. 

That’s when this heavy, gray feeling really started to settle in. I remember it was late fall, right before Thanksgiving, because I had to work through the holiday weekend just to get the new system running properly for my team. And ever since then... I just haven't been able to shake this exhaustion. It started as stress, I thought, just adjusting to the new role, but the stress never left, it just turned into this... this flatness. So, yes, three years and three months, give or take a week or two. It feels like a lifetime ago that I actually enjoyed my job, or anything else for that matter.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?

Well, no, not really. I mean, my husband hasn't said anything about me moving like molasses or anything like that. And he would, believe me, he would. He's always the first to point out if I'm doing something differently. Like, if I'm chopping vegetables for a salad and I'm not doing it exactly the way he thinks is most efficient, he'll swoop in and try to show me how to hold the knife. So if I were dragging my feet or talking in slow motion, he definitely would have mentioned it by now. 

And at work... well, I sit at a desk all day, like I said. So it's not like I'm running marathons around the office. Most of my communication is through emails or the messaging system they have set up on the new software platform. So people aren't really hearing me speak all that much anyway. When I do have to take a phone call—which I try to avoid these days because it just feels so draining to put on that 'customer service' voice—I think I sound the same. I've always been a fairly deliberate speaker. I don't rush my words, especially when I'm explaining policy details to someone who's just been in an accident and is already confused and upset. You have to be clear and methodical. So I don't think my speech has slowed down, it's just... well, it's always been measured, I suppose. 

As for moving slowly, I guess the only thing is that it takes me longer to get out of bed in the morning, but that's not because my body physically can't move faster. It's just that I don't want to. I lie there staring at the ceiling fan, watching the blades go round and round, just dreading having to put my feet on the floor and start the whole routine over again. But once I'm up, I move at my normal pace, I think. I make the coffee, I let the dog out, I shower... it's all just the same speed it's always been. So, no, I don't think I'm moving or speaking any slower. I just feel incredibly tired while I'm doing it all.
Do you find yourself fidgeting or restless, or feeling like you're stuck in place and can't seem to get moving, when you're not actively engaged in a task?

Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. I'm not a fidgety person at all. You know, some people, they just can't sit still—like my sister, for instance. Whenever we watch a movie, she's always bouncing her knee or picking at her cuticles or getting up to check her phone, but I've never been like that. When I finally get done with work and log off that awful computer system for the day, I usually just go sit in my recliner in the living room. It's this oversized brown leather one we bought at Macy's a few years ago, very comfortable, with the lumbar support. And when I sit there, I'm just... still. I'm not restless in the slightest. If anything, I'm just completely drained. 

I'll put on the evening news, or maybe Jeopardy—my husband loves Jeopardy, he always tries to guess the answers before the contestants, even though he's usually wrong, bless his heart—and I just sit there watching it. I don't feel any sort of nervous energy or the need to pace around the house or wring my hands or anything like that. 

And as for feeling stuck... well, it goes back to what I was saying about getting out of bed in the morning. It's not that my muscles won't work or that I'm literally glued to the chair. If the dog starts whining to go out in the yard, or if the oven timer goes off because my husband is trying to bake chicken, I can get up and handle it. I'm not paralyzed. It's just that I really, really don't *want* to get up unless I absolutely have to. I'd rather just stay put because doing anything else just takes so much effort. 

But it's not a physical inability to move, if that makes sense. It's just a complete lack of motivation to do so. I'm just... quiet. I just sit there, letting the evening pass by, watching the clock until it's an acceptable time to go to sleep. So, no, neither of those things really sound like me. I don't have any of that restless energy, and I'm not physically stuck. I'm just so worn out that sitting perfectly still is about the only thing that sounds appealing.
Has your current state of feeling tired and disconnected from activities been continuous over the past three years, or have you had periods where you felt somewhat better?

No, I really haven't. It's... it's honestly just been one long, uninterrupted stretch of feeling exactly like this. I keep waiting for it to lift, you know? Like, I'll think to myself, maybe when the weather warms up and spring finally gets here, I'll get a little bit of my old spark back. My husband always used to joke that I was like a solar panel, that I just needed a little sunshine to get going. But spring comes, and the flowers bloom, and then summer rolls around, and... nothing changes. I still feel just as heavy and drained as I did in the dead of winter. 

We even took a vacation last August. My husband's brother has this lovely little timeshare down in Myrtle Beach, right on the water, and we went down there for a week. Usually, I love the beach. I love sitting out there with a good book and just listening to the waves. I thought for sure that getting away from the office, getting away from that awful software system and the trainees and all the emails, that it would finally give me a break from this... this exhaustion. But it didn't. I just sat there on the balcony in South Carolina, staring out at the ocean, and I felt exactly the same as I do sitting in my recliner at home. Just completely flat. 

Even during the holidays, like Christmas... I used to love decorating the house, putting up the lights, baking, all of that. This past year, my husband brought all the boxes down from the attic, and I just looked at them and wanted to cry from how tired I was. I went through the motions and hung the ornaments because it's what you're supposed to do, but I didn't feel any joy or relief. It didn't feel like a break from the routine. So, no, there haven't been any good periods or days where I felt like my old self again. It's just been three years and three months of the exact same gray feeling, day in and day out, without any letup at all.
Have you lost any significant amount of weight over the past three years?

Oh, no, definitely not. I haven't lost any weight at all. In fact, my clothes fit exactly the same as they did three years ago. I still wear the exact same slacks... well, when I actually have to dress up, anyway. Most days I'm just in my comfortable pants since I'm sitting at the desk at home so much now. But no, no weight loss. 

My husband, bless him, he's the one who does most of the cooking these days because I'm just so completely drained by the time five o'clock rolls around. He makes a lot of really hearty meals, you know? He does a meatloaf, mashed potatoes, and he has this baked ziti recipe that is just loaded with ricotta and mozzarella cheese. He tries to make things he thinks will comfort me, I think, so we end up eating a lot of heavy, warm foods. And since I'm just sitting at that desk dealing with insurance claims all day, and then, like I said, moving straight to my recliner in the living room for the evening... I'm really not burning off anything. 

I mean, we go to the grocery store on Sunday mornings, usually the Kroger down the street, but even then, I'm just sort of leaning on the cart while he picks things out and compares the prices on canned goods. So, if anything, I might have even put on a pound or two over the winter, though I haven't actually stepped on the scale in our master bathroom for ages. I usually just wait until I have a doctor's appointment to find out, because looking at the numbers just feels like one more chore. But definitely no significant weight loss, no. I'm just carrying the exact same weight I always have.
Do you think your current state has affected your physical movements or activity level in any way?

Well, I don't really think my actual physical movements have changed, if that's what you mean. Like I was saying about going to Kroger or sitting in my recliner, it's not that I'm moving in slow motion or anything. When I do get up, I walk just the same as I always have. Like yesterday, my husband was out in the garage trying to fix the lawnmower—it's this old Toro that always gives him trouble when the grass starts getting long—and I realized I needed a refill on my coffee. I use this big ceramic mug my daughter got me for Mother's Day a few years back, the one with the painted daisies on it. Anyway, I got up from my desk, walked down the hall to the kitchen, poured my coffee, and walked back. I didn't feel like I was dragging my feet or wading through molasses or anything. It was just a normal walk down the hallway. I'm not clumsy, I'm not dropping my pen, my hands work just fine when I'm typing up those endless insurance claim reports. 

It's really just the *amount* of activity that's different, you know? Because I'm just so completely drained all the time, I just don't do as much. I used to go out and tend to the flower beds, or we'd take the dog for a long walk around the subdivision—we live in this nice little neighborhood with sidewalks and those pretty decorative streetlamps—but now, I just open the sliding glass door and let him out into the fenced backyard. So my overall activity level is definitely down, way down, just because I don't have the energy to do the things I used to do. But the actual, physical way my body moves? No, I haven't noticed anything strange or different there. I'm just doing a whole lot less moving overall.
Have you had any periods, no matter how brief, where you felt even slightly better or more like your old self since this all started three years ago?

Well, like I was trying to explain earlier when we were talking about the seasons changing and that trip to Myrtle Beach... no, I really haven't. It's funny you ask that again, because I actually spend a lot of time thinking about that very thing. I'll sit in my recliner in the evenings—it's this brown leather one we got at Rooms To Go about five years ago, right before they discontinued the model—and I'll try to rack my brain, just trying to pinpoint one single day, or even just an afternoon, where I felt like the old me. The me who used to organize the neighborhood block party or bake three dozen cookies for the church bake sale without even breaking a sweat. 

But no matter how hard I think about it, I just come up empty. There just hasn't been a break in the clouds, not even for a minute. Even on days that should be good, like my daughter's birthday back in October... we went to this Italian place she loves, the one downtown with the red-and-white checkered tablecloths and the really good garlic knots. I sat there, and everyone was laughing and telling stories, and my husband had ordered a nice bottle of Chianti, and I just felt... nothing. I mean, I smiled and nodded and ate my chicken parmesan, but inside, it was just the same heavy, gray exhaustion. I kept waiting for the atmosphere to rub off on me, you know? Like maybe if I just forced myself to participate, my brain would catch up and I'd feel a little spark of joy. But it never happened. It's just been this one long, continuous stretch of feeling completely flat and drained, day after day, for three whole years now. So, no, not even a brief period of feeling better. It's just always there.
Have you noticed any changes in how you feel about yourself or your worth as a person since you started feeling tired and disconnected?

Well, it's... I don't know if I'd say my actual feelings about my worth have changed, exactly. I mean, I know I'm still a good person. I know I'm a good mother to my daughter, and a good wife to my husband, even if he is doing most of the cooking these days with his meatloaf and baked ziti. I still do my job—I'm still processing those insurance claims every single day, sitting at that desk in the spare bedroom. We converted it into an office right when the pandemic started, painted it this soft sage green color because I read somewhere that green is supposed to be calming for a workspace. It has a nice window that looks out over the neighbor's rhododendrons, which are just beautiful in the spring, though I hardly ever really look at them anymore. 

But as far as my self-worth goes... I don't sit around thinking I'm a terrible person or that I'm worthless or anything like that. I don't hate myself. It's more just... I'm just so tired. I don't have the energy to feel much of anything about myself, good or bad. I just feel like I'm existing, you know? Just getting through the claims, getting through the dinner, getting to the recliner. I don't feel like a failure, I just feel... empty. And exhausted. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel differently about my worth as a person. I just don't really have the energy to think about it at all. It's just not something that crosses my mind when I'm so focused on just getting through the day.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed or lost interest in activities most of the day?

Well, like I was saying, it's just been this one long, continuous stretch for three years now. So... a period of two weeks? I mean, I guess you could say yes, because three years is certainly longer than two weeks, right? But it's not like it was just a two-week thing that came and went. It's not like I felt bad for fourteen days and then woke up on the fifteenth day feeling fine and ready to go plant petunias. It's just been this constant, steady, heavy tiredness and lack of interest in everything, every single day. 

Like I mentioned before, I don't even go out to the flower beds anymore, and I used to love doing that. I had this whole system for my bulbs, you know, making sure the tulips and daffodils were planted at just the right depth in the fall so they'd come up perfectly in the spring. I even had this special little kneeling pad I bought at a garden center out on Highway 9—it was memory foam, dark green, really saved my knees when I was pulling weeds. But I haven't used it in years. It's just sitting out in the garage somewhere, probably behind my husband's Toro lawnmower. 

So, yes, I've definitely had two weeks where I felt like this, but only because those two weeks are just a tiny drop in the bucket of the last three years. It's never stopped. There hasn't been a time where I *didn't* feel this way, where I didn't just want to finish my insurance claims and go sit in my brown leather recliner. So I wouldn't call it a "period" of two weeks, really. It's just... my life now. Just this endless, flat, exhausting routine.
Have you experienced significantly depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years?

Well, like I was just saying about the last three years... yes, definitely for more than two years. It's just this constant thing. Most days, it honestly just feels like there's this... this gray film over absolutely everything. It's like I'm looking at my life through a dirty window, you know? Even on the days when things are perfectly fine. Like, my husband will be so kind, bringing me a cup of Earl Grey tea while I'm working on those insurance claims in the spare room—he always uses that mug my daughter got me for Mother's Day five years ago, the one with the little painted daisies on it—and I know I should feel happy or grateful in that moment. Or when we're all in the kitchen and he's making his baked ziti and the house smells amazing, and my daughter is over and they're chatting... I can go through all the motions. I can stand there and stir the sauce and smile and say the right things, but I'm not really *feeling* any of the enjoyment I used to feel. It's just flat. I'm just going through the script, but the feeling behind it is just... blocked by that gray film. And that's been most of the day, pretty much every single day, for way longer than two years now. It's just exhausting to live like that, to never really feel the good parts of your own life anymore.
Have you lost interest in activities that you used to find enjoyable?

Well, like I was saying about the flower beds... yes, definitely. It's like everything I used to enjoy just feels like a chore now, or I just don't care about it at all. It's not just the gardening, either. I used to love reading. I had this whole collection of historical fiction novels—mostly about the Tudor period, you know, Henry VIII and all his wives. I had them all lined up alphabetically by author on this beautiful oak bookshelf my husband built for me in the living room. I used to be able to just sit in my recliner on a Sunday afternoon, with a cup of that Earl Grey tea, and get completely lost in a book for hours. I'd read about Anne Boleyn or Catherine of Aragon, and it felt like I was right there in the 1500s. 

But now? Now I can't even get through a single chapter. I'll pick up a book, read a page, and realize I haven't absorbed a single word. My eyes are just moving over the text, but my brain isn't taking it in. So I'll put it down and just turn on the TV instead, not even really watching whatever is on, just letting the noise fill the room. And it's the same with baking. I used to bake every weekend—my grandmother's recipe for lemon pound cake was my specialty. I had this vintage yellow Pyrex mixing bowl that I loved using for it. But I haven't baked that cake in... oh, it has to be at least two and a half years now. The thought of getting all the ingredients out, measuring the flour, zesting the lemons... it just feels like climbing Mount Everest. So, yes, all the things that used to bring me joy, the gardening, the reading, the baking... I just don't have any interest in them anymore. I just want to finish my claims, eat whatever my husband cooks, and go to sleep.
Have you experienced any restlessness or an inability to sit still, or on the other hand, felt like you're moving in slow motion?

No, I wouldn't say I feel restless or anything like that. I'm definitely not pacing around the house or tapping my foot or feeling like I can't sit still. In fact, like I mentioned, sitting still in my brown leather recliner is pretty much all I want to do these days. And I wouldn't say I'm moving in slow motion, either. I mean, I can still get up and walk to the kitchen to get a glass of water, or walk to the spare room to do my insurance claims, and I'm walking at a normal pace, I suppose. But it's not a physical inability to move, if that makes sense. It's just a complete lack of motivation to do so. I'm just... quiet. It's funny you ask that again, because I actually spend a lot of time thinking about that very thing. I'll sit in my recliner in the evenings—it's this brown leather one we got at Rooms To Go about five years ago, right before they discontinued the model—and I'll try to rack my brain, just trying to pinpoint one single day, or even just an afternoon, where I felt like the old me. The me who used to organize the neighborhood block party or bake three dozen cookies for the church bake sale without even breaking a sweat. 

But no matter how hard I think about it, I just come up empty. There just hasn't been a break in the clouds, not even for a minute. Even on days that should be good, like my daughter's birthday back in October... we went to this Italian place she loves, the one downtown with the red-and-white checkered tablecloths and the really good garlic knots. I sat there, and everyone was laughing and telling stories, and my husband had ordered a nice bottle of Chianti, and I just felt... nothing. I mean, I smiled and nodded and ate my chicken parmesan, but inside, it was just the same heavy, gray exhaustion. I kept waiting for the atmosphere to rub off on me, you know? Like maybe if I just forced myself to participate, my brain would catch up and I'd feel a little spark of joy. But it never happened. It's just been this one long, continuous stretch of feeling completely flat and drained, day after day, for three whole years now. So, no, not even a brief period of feeling better. It's just always there.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any significant changes in their self-esteem or self-worth over the past three years
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in how you feel about yourself or your worth as a person since you started feeling tired and disconnected?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of worthlessness or low self-esteem, which are not covered by any of the provided symptom profiles (Depressed_Mood, Fatigue, Hopelessness, functional_impairment, duration).

patient.answer:
Well, it's... I don't know if I'd say my actual feelings about my worth have changed, exactly. I mean, I know I'm still a good person. I know I'm a good mother to my daughter, and a good wife to my husband, even if he is doing most of the cooking these days with his meatloaf and baked ziti. I still do my job—I'm still processing those insurance claims every single day, sitting at that desk in the spare bedroom. We converted it into an office right when the pandemic started, painted it this soft sage green color because I read somewhere that green is supposed to be calming for a workspace. It has a nice window that looks out over the neighbor's rhododendrons, which are just beautiful in the spring, though I hardly ever really look at them anymore. 

But as far as my self-worth goes... I don't sit around thinking I'm a terrible person or that I'm worthless or anything like that. I don't hate myself. It's more just... I'm just so tired. I don't have the energy to feel much of anything about myself, good or bad. I just feel like I'm existing, you know? Just getting through the claims, getting through the dinner, getting to the recliner. I don't feel like a failure, I just feel... empty. And exhausted. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel differently about my worth as a person. I just don't really have the energy to think about it at all. It's just not something that crosses my mind when I'm so focused on just getting through the day.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of Major Depressive Episodes (a distinct period of at least two weeks with depressed mood or loss of interest). The patient's symptom profile includes Depressed Mood, Fatigue, Hopelessness, Functional Impairment, and Duration, but does not explicitly detail a past Major Depressive Episode or specify a distinct 2-week period of anhedonia/depression separate from the chronic PDD presentation.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was saying, it's just been this one long, continuous stretch for three years now. So... a period of two weeks? I mean, I guess you could say yes, because three years is certainly longer than two weeks, right? But it's not like it was just a two-week thing that came and went. It's not like I felt bad for fourteen days and then woke up on the fifteenth day feeling fine and ready to go plant petunias. It's just been this constant, steady, heavy tiredness and lack of interest in everything, every single day. 

Like I mentioned before, I don't even go out to the flower beds anymore, and I used to love doing that. I had this whole system for my bulbs, you know, making sure the tulips and daffodils were planted at just the right depth in the fall so they'd come up perfectly in the spring. I even had this special little kneeling pad I bought at a garden center out on Highway 9—it was memory foam, dark green, really saved my knees when I was pulling weeds. But I haven't used it in years. It's just sitting out in the garage somewhere, probably behind my husband's Toro lawnmower. 

So, yes, I've definitely had two weeks where I felt like this, but only because those two weeks are just a tiny drop in the bucket of the last three years. It's never stopped. There hasn't been a time where I *didn't* feel this way, where I didn't just want to finish my insurance claims and go sit in my brown leather recliner. So I wouldn't call it a "period" of two weeks, really. It's just... my life now. Just this endless, flat, exhausting routine.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition meets the criteria for a persistent depressive disorder
doctor.question: Have you experienced significantly depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most days I feel like there’s a gray film over everything, even when my husband is being kind or we’re cooking with the family, and I can go through the motions without really feeling the enjoyment I used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks if the patient has experienced a significantly depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years, which directly maps to the 'Depressed_Mood' symptom profile.

patient.answer: Well, like I was just saying about the last three years... yes, definitely for more than two years. It's just this constant thing. Most days, it honestly just feels like there's this... this gray film over absolutely everything. It's like I'm looking at my life through a dirty window, you know? Even on the days when things are perfectly fine. Like, my husband will be so kind, bringing me a cup of Earl Grey tea while I'm working on those insurance claims in the spare room—he always uses that mug my daughter got me for Mother's Day five years ago, the one with the little painted daisies on it—and I know I should feel happy or grateful in that moment. Or when we're all in the kitchen and he's making his baked ziti and the house smells amazing, and my daughter is over and they're chatting... I can go through all the motions. I can stand there and stir the sauce and smile and say the right things, but I'm not really *feeling* any of the enjoyment I used to feel. It's just flat. I'm just going through the script, but the feeling behind it is just... blocked by that gray film. And that's been most of the day, pretty much every single day, for way longer than two years now. It's just exhausting to live like that, to never really feel the good parts of your own life anymore.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced anhedonia
doctor.question: Have you lost interest in activities that you used to find enjoyable?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia (loss of interest in activities), which is not explicitly listed in the symptom profile. Functional Impairment mentions pulling back from painting, hiking, and volunteering, but the question is specifically asking about 'loss of interest' (anhedonia) as a symptom itself, which doesn't have a dedicated key in the provided profile.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was saying about the flower beds... yes, definitely. It's like everything I used to enjoy just feels like a chore now, or I just don't care about it at all. It's not just the gardening, either. I used to love reading. I had this whole collection of historical fiction novels—mostly about the Tudor period, you know, Henry VIII and all his wives. I had them all lined up alphabetically by author on this beautiful oak bookshelf my husband built for me in the living room. I used to be able to just sit in my recliner on a Sunday afternoon, with a cup of that Earl Grey tea, and get completely lost in a book for hours. I'd read about Anne Boleyn or Catherine of Aragon, and it felt like I was right there in the 1500s. 

But now? Now I can't even get through a single chapter. I'll pick up a book, read a page, and realize I haven't absorbed a single word. My eyes are just moving over the text, but my brain isn't taking it in. So I'll put it down and just turn on the TV instead, not even really watching whatever is on, just letting the noise fill the room. And it's the same with baking. I used to bake every weekend—my grandmother's recipe for lemon pound cake was my specialty. I had this vintage yellow Pyrex mixing bowl that I loved using for it. But I haven't baked that cake in... oh, it has to be at least two and a half years now. The thought of getting all the ingredients out, measuring the flour, zesting the lemons... it just feels like climbing Mount Everest. So, yes, all the things that used to bring me joy, the gardening, the reading, the baking... I just don't have any interest in them anymore. I just want to finish my claims, eat whatever my husband cooks, and go to sleep.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Have you experienced any restlessness or an inability to sit still, or on the other hand, felt like you're moving in slow motion?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor agitation or retardation (restlessness, inability to sit still, or moving in slow motion), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, I wouldn't say I feel restless or anything like that. I'm definitely not pacing around the house or tapping my foot or feeling like I can't sit still. In fact, like I mentioned, sitting still in my brown leather recliner is pretty much all I want to do these days. And I wouldn't say I'm moving in slow motion, either. I mean, I can still get up and walk to the kitchen to get a glass of water, or walk to the spare room to do my insurance claims, and I'm walking at a normal pace, I suppose. It's not like my body is physically moving slower than it used to. 

It's more just... a mental heaviness, if that makes sense? Like, the physical act of moving isn't slow, but the *motivation* to move is just completely drained out of me. When I'm sitting in that recliner, the thought of getting up to, say, go check the mail at the end of the driveway—which isn't even that far, it's just down past the big oak tree we planted when we first moved in twenty years ago—it just feels like such a monumental task. But once I actually force myself to stand up and do it, I'm walking normally. My husband hasn't said anything about me moving like a turtle or anything. He's very observant, too. He notices everything. Like last week, he noticed I hadn't been using my favorite lavender soap in the shower, the one he gets me from that little boutique downtown. He brought it up while we were eating dinner—he made his baked ziti again, which is always nice, even if I don't enjoy it like I used to—and he asked if I wanted him to pick up a different scent. So if I was moving in slow motion or acting restless, he definitely would have pointed it out to me by now. But no, physically, I think I'm moving at my normal speed, just... very reluctantly.
